newsitem.title: USA: Mississippi receives $170 million tobacco payment.
newsitem.headline: Mississippi receives $170 million tobacco payment.

text.p: Mississippi received a $170 million payment from the tobacco industry Tuesday, making the state the first in the nation to be compensated by major cigarette makers for the cost of treating ailing smokers.

Assistant Attorney General Trey Bobinger said the payment arrived in separate transfers from Philip Morris Cos. Inc., R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., and Lorillard Group Inc.
"This is a great day for the people of Mississippi. We have a great opportunity with this money to do some things," said Bobinger.
One use of the money proposed by state officials would be to provide health insurance for an estimated 100,000 children in Mississippi who currently have no protection.

But for the time being, the money was to remain in an escrow account at a SunTrust Bank branch in the Gulf Coast city of Pascagoula, where Attorney General Mike Moore first filed the state's landmark suit against the industry in 1994.

Thirty-nine other states subsequently brought their own suits seeking compensation from tobacco companies for Medicaid funds spent on smoking-related illnesses. The result was last month's $368.5 billion national tobacco settlement.

Tuesday's payment to Mississippi was part of a $3.4 billion 25-year settlement intended to guarantee payments to the state should the national deal fall through. The settlement's size dwarfed the $940 million that Mississippi had initially sought in damages.

Under its terms, Mississippi would receive another $68 million next year and $76.5 million in 1999. Annual payments would rise to $136 million by the sixth year of the settlement and remain at that level.
A ruling on how the first payment could be distributed was expected soon from a county judge but the state legislature would have the final say in how the money would be spent.

"One possibility is to provide health-care coverage for children, possibly an expansion of our Medicaid programme, improve anti-tobacco educational programmes in the school system. I could go on and on," said Bobinger.
Moore was in Washington Tuesday to work out details of the payment transfer and to lobby Congress on behalf of the national agreement. He was not available for comment.
Tobacco opponents said Tuesday's payment to Mississippi represented a milestone.

"This is unconditional hard, cold cash being paid to settle a specific case, something the tobacco companies always said they would never do," said Richard Daynard, Northeastern Univerity law professor and chairman of the Tobacco Products Liability Project in Boston.

"With the exception of Liggett's voluntary settlement, the industry never paid out anything and were very proud of it. In fact, they used this very deliberatrely as a strategyy to discourage lawsuits," he said.
Liggett Group became the first cigarette maker to pay money to settle lawsuits in April 1996, when it broke ranks with other tobacco companies.
